title: World Cinema Radar — the podcast, Saturday 7 November 2026

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to World Cinema Radar, the podcast. I'm {A}, and today is Saturday the seventh of November, twenty twenty-six.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm {B}. <chuckle> Saturday morning, coffee in hand, and a fresh edition to go through.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Today has three main threads. First, a big announcement from the world of anime adaptations: Sony joins Lionsgate on a live-action Naruto.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Second, a change at the top of Pixar, which is a bigger deal than it sounds. And third, the weekend listings in Spanish cinemas, with four films worth talking about.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We also have the Tallinn festival, opera streaming dates, and the calendar for the next few weeks.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A quick note on how we work. Everything we say comes from the written edition, and where the sources are thin, we tell you.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which is the case today for two stories. <chuckle> We'd rather say less than say something we can't check.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. So you'll hear a few careful phrases. That's on purpose.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right, and it's why you can trust the dates. Every date is for Spain unless we say otherwise.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Honestly? A good mix. Let's start.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, Naruto. The manga that a whole generation grew up with. Sony Pictures is joining Lionsgate to co-finance and distribute the live-action film.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: |Wait, Lionsgate already had it?| Yes, they have been developing it for a while. The director is Destin Daniel Cretton, the man behind Shang-Chi.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And he is also writing and producing. He was attached back in twenty twenty-four, so this isn't a new name, it's a new partner with more money.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the key point. Sony's arrival suggests the project is moving from talk to real preparation. The report says filming would start in spring twenty twenty-seven.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, let's be careful here. The report comes from The Hollywood Reporter, but the pieces we could read were secondary, so the Radar marks it as a single, unofficial source.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Good caution. And there is no cast yet. Nobody has been named for Naruto himself, and there's no release date.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, nothing to get excited about in terms of faces. <chuckle> Only the structure: Lionsgate runs development, production and domestic distribution, and Sony helps pay.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Does it fit the profile? Not really, <short pause> I'd say it's a curiosity rather than a priority. But anime adaptations in live-action are a big industrial trend, so it's worth tracking.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Agreed. A Japanese story, a Hollywood budget. We'll report when there's a cast.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And a small note. The film is Japanese in origin, so it sits fine with our rules. Nothing Indian here.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let me add one more thing about the industry side. When a studio brings a partner in, it usually spreads the risk.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Sure. A big adaptation costs a lot, and Naruto has a huge global audience. So sharing the bill makes sense.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But we don't have the budget, because nobody has reported one. We won't guess.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: No guesses. <short pause> What we know is short: studios, director, the spring start. That's it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And that already makes it a story, because a start date for filming means the script and the plan are advanced.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Though a start date is also a plan, and plans move. We'll watch for changes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If you follow anime, keep this one on your list. If you don't, you can leave it for now.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fair advice.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So the short version for listeners: Naruto live-action, Sony and Lionsgate, Cretton directing, filming in spring twenty twenty-seven.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the long version is in the edition, with the sources and the caveats.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. Next story.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now Pixar. Jim Morris, the studio president for twelve years, is stepping back.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Announced on the fourth of November. He becomes president emeritus, and Jonathan Garson takes over on the fourth of January, twenty twenty-seven.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Garson has been at Disney for more than thirty years, and at Pixar since twenty ten. So it's an insider.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Yes. And the creative side doesn't move much. Pete Docter stays as chief creative officer and keeps oversight of the films. Jonas Rivera becomes executive vice president of creative.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: What happens to Morris himself? <breath> He remains executive producer on Incredibles 3, and he'll focus on talent development, mentoring and technology.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Disney's Alan Bergman called it succession planning, an orderly handover to ensure a smooth transition. No retirement date was announced.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And here is the interesting bit. The report we read says none of the outlets linked the move to Pixar's recent box office misses.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, as far as we can tell, there's no sign of a crisis. Deadline reportedly said the transition was always in the works.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Reuters added that Pixar says its films grossed more than twelve billion dollars during Morris' time.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Big numbers. <giggle> Though again, we must say we read one summary, not the original notes, so treat the details with a little care.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fair. For a film lover it means one thing: the creative leadership continues. That's the part that matters on screen.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One more point on Pixar. Handovers like this are often read as bad news.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And here the sources say the opposite: it was planned, and the creative leaders stay in place.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Pete Docter is the one who really shapes the films, so for audiences the practical effect is small.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The practical effect is mostly on the business side. Garson will oversee production and operations.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Production and operations. So the schedule, the budgets, the machine behind the films.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Yes. And Morris moves into mentoring, which sounds like a gentle exit. <giggle>

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A very Pixar way to leave, in a way. Nothing dramatic.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We'll come back if there's any change after January.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Short version again: Garson in January, Docter stays, Morris becomes emeritus.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And no link to the box office, at least not in what we read.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. On to the weekend.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Okay, the weekend listings. These films opened on Friday in Spain, and today we have more details: casts and running times.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Let's start with Sacamantecas, by David P. Sañudo. A historical thriller, a hundred and nine minutes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's set in Álava, during the Third Carlist War. Women are found strangled near Vitoria, and the chief of the constables is under pressure to hide it all.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The cast is strong: Antonio de la Torre, Patricia López Arnaiz and Luis Callejo. |That's a serious cast.|

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a local review calls it a beautiful film about grief versus silence. I like that phrase.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It has a dark, period feel, which hits two items on the profile at once: historical cinema and a touch of horror.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then there's Ruega por nosotras, by Daniel Monzón. A hundred and thirty-six minutes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Nineteen seventy-four. A rebellious nineteen-year-old is sent to a reformatory with a brutal disciplinary regime. She finds support among the other girls.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Monzón is a director who knows how to hold a long drama. We haven't seen it, though, so we'll only say what the synopsis promises.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. Next, the big one by length. Los miserables, by Fred Cavayé. A hundred and seventy-eight minutes.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: <chuckle> Three hours. Vincent Lindon plays Valjean, Tahar Rahim is Javert, and there's also Camille Cottin.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One review says it's a story worth returning to. It's a new adaptation of Victor Hugo, so the question is whether it brings something fresh.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd say the length is a risk and a promise at the same time. Some people want the long, faithful version.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the fourth: Godzilla Minus Zero, by Takashi Yamazaki. A hundred and thirty-five minutes. The sequel to Godzilla Minus One.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Japan, two years after the war, still rebuilding, and a new threat appears.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The first one was a surprise for many people. So the expectations are high. |No way, a sequel that people actually want.| <laugh>

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let's mention the rest. Fiesta Pagäna, a biopic of the band Mägo de Oz. The Catalan horror film eleven. And some family films.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And there's an Indian epic, Ramayana, that we leave out. It's the reader's decision.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: All these dates are for Spain, of course. Nothing is deduced from other countries.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let me go back to Sacamantecas for a moment, because its subject is strong. A real kind of dread, with a historical frame.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We should say that we haven't watched it. We only read descriptions and a review headline, so we won't pretend.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Agreed. Still, the pairing of De la Torre and López Arnaiz is a good sign on paper.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: On paper. <chuckle> Everything is good on paper.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And for Los miserables, a hundred and seventy-eight minutes means you plan your evening around it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Bring snacks. |Three hours and some.|

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For Ruega por nosotras, the period setting is the draw. Nineteen seventy-four, a reformatory, a strict regime.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It sounds heavy, but the synopsis also talks about friendship among the girls, so there's warmth in it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Godzilla Minus Zero might be the easiest sell for a crowd. It's the biggest spectacle of the four.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And it's Japanese, from Yamazaki, who also made the first one. So there's continuity.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If you can only pick one, it depends on the mood. History, drama, or monsters.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd start with Sacamantecas. Short, tense, historical. <short pause> But that's me.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One thing I appreciate is that the Radar separates the Spanish dates from everything else.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, a film can open in Japan or the United States weeks earlier, and that tells you nothing about Spain.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Godzilla Minus Zero is a good example, because it reached other places first.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And now it's here, so people can finally stop avoiding spoilers online. <laugh>

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Which, to be clear, we don't give you. No spoilers on the Radar.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Never. We stay with the setup, the cast and the running time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the point of the section. Four solid choices for one weekend.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now to Estonia. The Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, or PÖFF, is thirty years old.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It opened on the sixth of November with Ulya, by the Latvian director Viesturs Kairišs.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A co-production between Latvia, Estonia, Poland and Lithuania. It played in Un Certain Regard at Cannes, and it's Latvia's Oscar submission, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The festival's own site confirms that the thirtieth edition began on opening day.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the competition has twelve films from fifteen countries, with the screenwriter and director Christopher Hampton as jury president, says Cineuropa.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Yesterday we described the whole programme. Today we only add the opening film.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The festival runs until the twenty-second of November, so the awards come at the closing.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a reminder: a festival title isn't a release. Nothing here says a film will reach Spain.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What I like about Tallinn is how it mixes big names and small discoveries.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: This year the opening film has already been through Cannes, so it comes with a reputation.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Being a national Oscar submission also says something about how Latvia sees the film.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It does. And four countries co-produced it, which is typical of the Baltic region.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We don't have a Spanish release date, so for now it's a film to remember.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The festival also has an industry side, but we haven't verified anything on that today, so we leave it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Next week we may have the first reactions from the competition.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Short version: thirty years, twelve competition films, Hampton as jury president, awards on the twenty-second.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We'll be back with the winners.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. We'll keep following it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Our stage section. Today, no new complete recording with access from Spain, so we'll talk about what's coming.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: OperaVision lists Šárka, by Janáček, from the National Theatre Brno, on the fifteenth of November at seven in the evening, Central European time.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then the International Opera Awards on the twenty-first, two family titles on the twenty-second, and Britten's Peter Grimes on the twenty-sixth, from the Finnish National Opera and Ballet.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Le Roi d'Ys and De Materie appear in a last chance to watch list. |So hurry if you wanted them.|

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But the page doesn't say about subtitles or when things expire. So, careful.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And then there's Carmen, the Damiano Michieletto production from the Royal Ballet and Opera. It reaches cinemas on the tenth of November.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Sesto Quatrini conducts, with Ginger Costa-Jackson and Russell Thomas. But Trafalgar Releasing says availability is international, without naming Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So we don't know whether Spanish cinemas will show it. <sigh> We'll keep following it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A word on Carmen. Michieletto's production is known for its modern setting.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: We should be careful there; today's sources only give the cast, the conductor and the date, so I'll stay with those.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Good point. The runtime was not listed on the page we read, so we don't give one.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For Spanish readers the real question is whether a chain will show it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the answer today is: not confirmed. <sigh> We'll look again closer to the tenth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Meanwhile OperaVision is the dependable option, because it's free and it's online.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Free? The page we read doesn't say that, so let's not promise it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: You're right, thank you. We only know the dates and the titles.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And we don't call it a complete recording with access from Spain, because we can't verify that.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Quick calendar. This weekend, the Spanish listings we just discussed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Tuesday the tenth, the Carmen in cinemas, not confirmed for Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Sunday the fifteenth, Šárka on OperaVision. And Tallinn runs until the twenty-second.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The twenty-sixth, Peter Grimes. And on the fourth of January, Garson takes over at Pixar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Notice how the calendar is short today, because the week is quiet on confirmed dates.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Short, but useful. Mark the tenth, the fifteenth and the twenty-sixth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And remember the tenth is only for cinemas that confirm the Carmen. Not necessarily in Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. We will repeat that when we know more.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Spring twenty twenty-seven, the start of filming for Naruto.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Our picks. First, Sacamantecas. Editorial affinity four out of five, medium confidence.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A historical thriller with a good cast and a favourable local review. We haven't seen it, remember.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then Los miserables, affinity three out of five, medium confidence. A big period drama, a hundred and seventy-eight minutes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And Ruega por nosotras, three out of five, low confidence, because we only have the synopsis.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Remember, this is editorial affinity. It isn't the critics' score or the public's.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If I had to choose one for tonight, it would be Sacamantecas.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd go for Los miserables if I had a whole free afternoon.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And Ruega por nosotras for a quieter evening.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: All three are in Spanish cinemas now, so there's no waiting.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Today we verified nothing on physical editions or streaming, so no picks there.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, the idea of the day. A weekend of strong listings in Spain, a handover at Pixar, and a festival starting in the Baltic.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And one anime adaptation that is still looking for its cast. <chuckle> The full edition has all the sources.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Thanks for listening. See you tomorrow on the Radar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One last thought before we go: a quiet news day is a good day to actually watch something.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Hear, hear. <chuckle> Pick a film, switch off the phone, and enjoy it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Bye!
